content: Manganese, when consumed or inhaled in excessive amounts, is toxic, similar to most metals. However, in appropriate quantities, manganese plays a critical role in human physiology. It is an essential component of certain enzymes and facilitates the development and activity of other enzymes. One of the most important manganese-dependent enzymes is manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), which serves as the primary antioxidant within mitochondria, protecting cells from oxidative damage. Manganese-activated enzymes are involved in the metabolism of carbohydrates, amino acids, and cholesterol. A deficiency in manganese can lead to skeletal deformities in animals and impair collagen production, which is crucial for wound healing. Additionally, high dietary intake of other minerals, such as iron, magnesium, and calcium, can interfere with the proper absorption of manganese. Dietary sources of manganese include leafy green vegetables, fruits, nuts, and whole grains. However, in processed grains like white bread, the nutrient-rich wheat germ, which contains the majority of the grain's minerals and vitamins, is often removed due to its darker color and perceived impurity. This wheat germ is typically repurposed as livestock feed. Many common vitamin and mineral supplements fail to include manganese in their formulations, potentially contributing to deficiencies. From a health perspective, some nutritionists associate manganese deficiency with a range of conditions, including joint pain, inflammation, arthritis, bursitis, dermatitis, and diseases such as Parkinson's disease, osteoporosis, schizophrenia, diabetes, and epilepsy.
